title: Agentic GraphRAG: Simplifying Retrieval Across Structured & Unstructured Data — Zach Blumenfeld

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

summary:
Zach Blumenfeld presents GraphRAG as a solution for simplifying retrieval across both structured and unstructured data sources in agentic workflows. He argues that as agents increasingly decompose questions into multiple queries rather than performing straight vector searches, a knowledge graph placed in the middle of the architecture provides significant value for accuracy, explainability, and controllability.

The demonstration centers on an employee skills assistant built for a fictional company (Cyberdine Systems). The initial data consists of PDF résumés. Blumenfeld first loads these as document chunks with embeddings into Neo4j, then builds an agent using Google's ADK framework with a document search tool. This baseline approach fails on multiple fronts: asking how many Python developers exist incorrectly returns 5 (because K=5 was set for retrieval), similarity search relies on loose semantic matching, and aggregation questions like summarizing skills distribution cannot be answered because document search cannot perform aggregations.

To solve this, Blumenfeld performs entity extraction using Pydantic classes with enumerations for accomplishment types, domains, and work types, and uses LangChain to decompose documents into JSON. This creates a more expressive graph data model connecting people to skills and accomplishments, with accomplishments linked to higher-level domains and work types. He then creates a new agent using an MCP server that reads the graph schema and generates Cypher queries. With this setup, the same questions yield accurate results: 28 Python developers, precise similarity calculations based on skill overlap, and proper aggregation of skills distribution with explainable numbers across domains.

Blumenfeld further demonstrates the flexibility of graph data models when adding new data. When internal HR intelligence system data about project collaborations is introduced, the graph accommodates new many-to-many relationships without the schema refactoring that tabular (RDBMS) systems would require—no join tables needed, just new relationships. This flexibility is crucial as agent systems evolve quickly and need to ingest new data rapidly. He creates a collaborator-finding tool using Cypher match queries and demonstrates that questions about who collaborated on AI projects return specific, data-grounded answers (e.g., Sarah and Amanda collaborated on specific projects). The graph structure also enables flexible multi-hop traversals (0-3 hops) across skills, systems, domains, and accomplishments for finding similar people.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Graph Architecture Overview
sections.summary: Blumenfeld introduces GraphRAG for multiple data sources and presents a general architecture with agents, tools, and a knowledge graph in the middle that can ingest both unstructured documents and structured ETL data. He emphasizes the value for agentic workflows where questions are decomposed into multiple queries.

sections.title: Baseline Document-Only Approach and Failures
sections.summary: Loads résumé PDFs as document chunks with embeddings into Neo4j and builds an agent in Google ADK with a document search tool. Demonstrates failures: counting Python developers returns 5 (K=5), similarity search lacks precision, and aggregation and collaboration questions cannot be answered with vector search alone.

sections.title: Entity Extraction and Graph Data Model Construction
sections.summary: Explains the desired data model (person, skills, accomplishments) and uses Pydantic classes with enumerations for accomplishment types, domains, and work types. LangChain decomposes documents into JSON containing skills and accomplishments, which are loaded into Neo4j to create an expressive graph connecting people, skills, and accomplishment types.

sections.title: Graph-Based Querying Results and Multi-hop Traversal
sections.summary: Creates a new agent with an MCP server that reads schema and generates Cypher. Demonstrates improved results: 28 Python developers, precise similarity calculation (Sarah closest to Lucas based on skill overlap), and proper skills distribution aggregation. Shows flexible multi-hop traversal queries (0-3 hops) across skills, systems, domains, and accomplishments for finding similar people.

sections.title: Explainability, Adding Collaboration Data, and Graph Schema Flexibility
sections.summary: Shows explainable similarity results for Lucas Martinez with specific numbers across skills and domains. Then demonstrates adding HR intelligence system data about project collaborations to the graph. Contrasts graph with RDBMS/tabular systems, noting that graph requires no join tables or schema refactoring when moving from one-to-many to many-to-many relationships—just new relationships. Creates a collaborator-finding tool with Cypher match queries and demonstrates queries about who collaborated on AI projects, returning specific results (Sarah and Amanda). Emphasizes graph flexibility is crucial for fast-moving agent systems.
